items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: Marshall Stearns, you look up his articles in Downbeat in 1936, he says, we ought to find a different expression than jazz for the music... That's what Marshall Stearns had. He tried to change the name.

ctx.x: And I think possibly your best records are made on this side.

On this side. The Victor's got the best records and the Victor company, I asked them for permission to re-dub them records and they told me that they come from their legal department that they kept them in their vault. They called them some kind of record vault. And my hands was tied. I was going to take a chance and put them out myself to combat this propaganda that these other men were putting out. You see, they have an organization that make money at this thing called the Jazz Club. The very word they use is…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: This thing was started by one Marshall Stearns, a young Jewish scholar not out of school, who wrote lies about me and my band

ctx.x: Well, that'll show you what kind of people that the jazz club has and at the head of it. He wrote me in 1949 that I have proof that we were the original Dixieland jazz band. Now he's writing up on this guy that he is the original Dixieland jazz band. They give him a cup for his presence of being in the jazz club. What wonderful people they have in New Orleans. All they were doing was to start integration, what they call the mixing bowl. They had started that up north 22 years ago, 20 years ago, by Marshall Stein.…

This is a letter headed Dominique James Nicola Rocca, 2218 Constant Street, New Orleans, Louisiana, 13, January the 9th, 1955. Senator Eastland of Mississippi, Washington, D.C. Honorable Senator Eastland, Hoping you may direct your committee attention to the propaganda that has been going on in New Orleans. Because wherever there is smoke, there must be fire. These people have given out history, read jazz music, as compiled by the Northern Coppetbaggers, NAACP through Bill Handy, trying to give the Negro culture…
I want you to read this here about a nine-man court.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: The interviewee discusses Marshall Stearns in the context of a letter and historical arguments about jazz history, but does not describe a personal meeting, collaboration, or direct professional relationship, only referencing Stearns as a historian/author who wrote about him.

ctx.x: You know, that's all. Not only the Louisiana Five, but everybody. It was a field lead from the all steel music and different things out the original Dixieland jazz band. Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on. Because he didn't know no better. He was just a Negro that didn't know no better. Like these even white crumbs who's supposed to be historians around New Orleans. They…

The letter here from... Let me see. I'll give you the full letterhead. It's a letter from Marshall W. Stearns. Yale Hot Club, 6th Linwood Place, New Haven, Connecticut. M. W. Stearns, President. Charter Unit of the UHCA. January the 11th, 1937, Mr. D.J. La Rocca, Earl Theater, Washington, D.C. Dear Nick, I have all your records from Liberty Stable Blues to the recent disc. I like the earlier ones better. Between you and me, our last argument should furnish you with plenty of publicity. I do think, however, that…

From this article, many other articles was copied. This is a work, you've got to be either pro-communist or a communist to work this way. There's a letter to keep me quiet. I'm a working man, trying to support a family. This man has not stopped writing about Negroes, yet he knows different. Now here's Brown's letter. To show you Brown was lying, I want to show you, I want to have him read this in there, what the name of his band was, in case you ever read Downbeat on 1936, and see what they have did to a man who…
